title: The Library Card Is a Financial Instrument Nobody Prices
body: Last year I did something boring and radical. For every book I wanted, I borrowed it from the library first, and only bought it if I had finished it and knew I would reread it. Twelve months later the arithmetic is embarrassing for my old self, and the side effects were worth more than the savings. Here is the whole ledger. The money first, because money is the language everybody hears. I finished thirty-one books. At my country's prices, owning those would have cost me somewhere around four hundred and sixty units of currency, plus the shelf I would have needed to store them. I bought five of the thirty-one, spending about eighty. The library charged me nothing; it is funded by taxes I already pay, which makes the marginal cost of a borrowed book effectively zero. Net saving. About three hundred and eighty, or, to phrase it the way that actually changed my behavior, four hundred and sixty minus eighty equals a month of groceries I did not have to think about. But the hidden returns were better. Borrowing converts buying mistakes into free ones. Under the old regime, a book that disappointed me after forty pages still lived in my house forever, a small monument to sunk cost, and its presence made me feel obligated. Under the new regime, a disappointing book goes back in the return slot and costs me nothing but the forty pages. I abandoned eleven books this year without a shred of guilt, and abandoning bad books is a skill, because life is short and the return slot is right there. When everything is cheap to quit, you get brave about starting. The deadlines do something to reading that ownership cannot. A borrowed book has a due date, and a due date is a gentle, external, honest force. I finished books this year that under the old regime would have drifted to the middle of the shelf and stayed there for a decade, because the library said Tuesday and Tuesday does not negotiate. Three of the five books I ended up buying were books I had already finished under deadline pressure and then re-borrowed, which is the strongest possible signal that a book is truly mine. There is also the shelf question. My bookshelf now holds five books I love instead of thirty-one I sort of remember. Guests pick up any of the five and every one of them is a recommendation with a reason attached. A shelf of kept promises beats a warehouse of intentions. The library itself turned out to be an underused building. Free warm space, desks with lamps, a machine that prints for pennies, a librarian who knows things search engines do not rank, and other humans quietly doing their work nearby, which turns out to be a genuine productivity technology. I now write there one morning a week. Nobody has ever tried to sell me anything in that building, which in this economy is practically a nature reserve. The honest costs, so you can weigh them fairly. New releases sometimes have a waiting list, which I have reframed as a reading queue that costs nothing and always has a next item ready. Some books I wanted were not in the system, and I requested two of them, and the library bought both, which means my taxes literally commissioned the exact book I asked for, a form of representation I did not expect to enjoy this much. Get the card. It takes ten minutes and one utility bill. Then run the same experiment for one year. Borrow first, buy only the keepers. The worst case is you read more and spend less. The best case is the one I hit. Your shelf becomes honest, your guilt about unfinished books disappears, and a building near you starts working for you the way it was always meant to.
